unit.subtitle: Jewish beliefs about God, Torah and Covenant, alongside the practices of Shabbat, kashrut and life-cycle.

lessons.title: Jewish Beliefs about God and Sacred Place
lessons.description: One God, the Shema, transcendence and judgement, the synagogue and the Jewish home.
lessons.content_html:
Jewish Belief in One G-d

At the heart of Judaism is monotheism — the belief in one God and one God alone. The Torah opens with the declaration that G-d created the heavens and the earth, establishing from the first verse that all existence depends on this one creator. Genesis 1:3–5 describes G-d bringing light into being through speech alone, conveying an unlimited creative power that requires no materials or assistance. Exodus 20:1–17, the Ten Commandments, begins with G-d identifying himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — linking belief in one God to the history of a real community.

Jewish belief in G-d is not abstract. G-d is understood as omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent (present everywhere), and omnibenevolent (all-loving and good). G-d is also eternal, existing outside time and not subject to change or decay. These qualities distinguish the Jewish God from the gods of surrounding ancient peoples, who were often depicted as limited, rivalrous, or morally flawed.

Key Fact

The Shema is the most important prayer in Judaism, drawn from Deuteronomy 6:4. It declares that G-d is one — a statement of absolute monotheism. Observant Jews recite it in the morning and the evening.

G-d as Transcendent, Merciful, and Judge

Judaism teaches that G-d is transcendent — wholly beyond the created order, not contained within it. Isaiah 55:8–9 expresses this powerfully, declaring that G-d’s thoughts and ways are higher than human thoughts and ways, as the heavens are higher than the earth. This means G-d cannot be fully comprehended by human reason alone, and visual representations of G-d are forbidden.

Yet G-d is also personal and relational. Jewish tradition emphasises G-d’s mercy (rachamim) alongside justice. G-d forgives those who genuinely repent, and the annual cycle of festivals includes Rosh Hashanah (the Day of Judgement) and Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement), when Jews seek forgiveness. G-d as eternal judge means that human moral choices have ultimate significance — G-d rewards the righteous and punishes wrongdoing, though divine mercy always accompanies divine justice in Jewish theology.

Because G-d is so far beyond human understanding, Jewish tradition exercises great care with the divine name. Many observant Jews write “G-d” instead of the full word, and the four Hebrew letters of the divine name (the Tetragrammaton, YHWH) are not pronounced as written. When reading the Torah aloud, Jews substitute “Adonai” (Lord) for the written name.

The synagogue serves four functions in Jewish life: prayer, study, celebration, and assembly. It is not considered sacred in the way a Temple was sacred; rather, it is the community that makes the place holy. This means synagogues vary enormously in design, from ornate Victorian buildings to converted terraced houses.

Key features of the synagogue include: the aron hakodesh (the ark), a cabinet at the front wall containing the Torah scrolls; the ner tamid (the eternal light), a lamp that burns continuously above or in front of the ark, representing G-d’s constant presence; the bimah, a raised platform from which the Torah is read; and displayed text of the Ten Commandments, often above the ark. Seating arrangements differ between traditions: in Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately; in Reform and Liberal synagogues, they sit together.

Orthodox, Reform, and Liberal Judaism differ significantly in synagogue practice. In Orthodox synagogues, services are conducted primarily in Hebrew, led by a male rabbi, and women do not read from the Torah in the main service. Reform and Liberal synagogues use more English in services, ordain female rabbis, and allow mixed seating. These differences reflect wider debates about how Jewish law (halakha) should be interpreted in the modern world.

The Home as a Place of Worship

In Jewish life, the home is as important as the synagogue. The philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel described the Sabbath as a “cathedral in time” — and much of Jewish religious life is practised within the family home rather than in a communal building. This emphasis on domestic faith means that Jewish identity is transmitted across generations primarily through family practice.

A visible sign of this is the mezuzah, a small case attached to the doorpost of Jewish homes (and often of every room), containing a handwritten parchment with verses from Deuteronomy including the Shema. Touching the mezuzah and kissing one’s fingers upon entering and leaving reminds the family of G-d’s presence in everyday life.

The home is especially central to Shabbat observance. Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and ends at nightfall on Saturday, following the commandment in Exodus 20:8–10 to remember the Sabbath and keep it holy. The family lights candles, says blessings over wine (kiddush) and bread (challah), and abstains from creative work. Shabbat creates a weekly rhythm of rest that re-centres Jewish life on G-d. The challenges of observing Shabbat fully — not driving, not using electronic devices, not cooking — are real in modern Britain, and different families and communities navigate them differently.

Key Fact

The mezuzah (doorpost case) and Shabbat candles are two key ways Jewish domestic space expresses faith. Observing Shabbat at home is commanded in Exodus 20:8–10: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”

Because G-d is transcendent — entirely beyond the material world — Judaism forbids any artistic representation of G-d. Images or statues would reduce the infinite to something finite and manageable, which would misrepresent G-d’s true nature. This shapes synagogue decoration: Hebrew calligraphy, geometric patterns, and symbolic imagery replace figurative art. The Shema displayed in beautiful script makes language the medium for divine encounter.

The kippah (skullcap) worn by many Jewish men is a visible reminder that G-d is above, watching over the person’s actions. The tallit (prayer shawl) is worn during morning prayer; its fringes (tzitzit) remind the wearer of all 613 commandments. These practices embed awareness of G-d’s presence into daily bodily routine.

>
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about Jewish beliefs about G-d, examiners want you to go beyond description and explain the religious significance of each attribute. For example, do not just say ‘Jews believe G-d is transcendent’ — add that this is why images of G-d are forbidden and why the divine name is written as ‘G-d.’ For the 8-mark ‘Explain Two Beliefs’ question, pair each belief with a source of wisdom: Deuteronomy 6:4 (the Shema), Isaiah 55:8–9 (transcendence), or Genesis 1:3–5 (omnipotence shown in creation). For the 15-mark evaluation, distinguish between Orthodox and Reform interpretations to show religious diversity within Judaism.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Judaism is strictly monotheistic. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) declares G-d’s absolute oneness. G-d is understood as omnipotent, omnipresent, omnibenevolent, eternal, transcendent (Isaiah 55:8–9), merciful, and judge.
  • The synagogue serves as a place for prayer, study, celebration, and assembly. Key features include the aron hakodesh (Torah ark), ner tamid (eternal light), and bimah (reading platform). Orthodox, Reform, and Liberal synagogues differ in language, gender roles, and interpretation of law.
  • The home is central to Jewish religious life. The mezuzah marks it as a sacred space, and Shabbat observance — commanded in Exodus 20:8–10 — transforms the domestic environment into a weekly act of worship and identity.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) G-d is transcendent — Isaiah 55:8-9 says G-d's ways are higher than human ways, which is why images are forbidden; (2) G-d is the eternal judge — reward and punishment are built into the moral order, seen in the High Holy Days. practice_questions.text: 'The synagogue is more important than the home for Jewish worship.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: synagogue is the communal centre for prayer, Torah reading, and lifecycle events; Orthodox Judaism requires minyan (quorum of ten) for certain prayers. Disagree: home is where Shabbat is observed, mezuzah marks sacred space, and faith is transmitted to children; historically, synagogues were not always available (diaspora). Non-religious view: neither has spiritual significance; community and family bonds are equally achievable without religious buildings or rituals. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with two or more sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or weak sources. Emerging: Simple assertion.

lessons.title: Jewish Practices: Worship, Shabbat and Kashrut
lessons.description: The Shema, kippah, tallith, synagogue interior, Shabbat observance and kosher food laws explained.
lessons.content_html:
The Centrality of Practice in Jewish Life

Judaism is a religion of practice as much as belief. The 613 commandments (mitzvot) of the Torah cover every aspect of daily life — from prayer and worship to what a Jew eats and how they rest. These practices are not arbitrary rules but expressions of the covenant between God and the Jewish people: each act of observance is a way of honouring and remembering that relationship. This lesson explores three of the most important areas of Jewish practice: worship (including the Shema, the kippah and the tallith), the synagogue, and the laws of Shabbat and kashrut.

The Shema: The Heart of Jewish Worship

The most fundamental Jewish prayer is the Shema (from the Hebrew word meaning ‘hear’). It begins: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad — ‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one.’ This is the Jewish affirmation of monotheism: God is absolutely one, undivided, unique. Observant Jews recite the Shema in the morning and evening as commanded, and many recite it as the last words before sleep or at the point of death.

The Shema is not merely a doctrinal statement but an act of devotion. The tradition teaches that when reciting it, one should concentrate fully on the meaning of each word, particularly the word echad (one), drawing out its sound as a sign of intention. The Shema comes from the book of Deuteronomy and is followed by two other Torah passages that together make up the full Shema liturgy. Because Judaism holds that God’s name is supremely holy, many Jews write ‘G-d’ in English correspondence — deliberately incomplete as a sign of reverence.

The Kippah and the Tallith

The kippah (also called a yarmulke) is a small head covering worn by Jewish men. Its purpose is to signify that there is always something ‘above’ the wearer — a constant, physical reminder of God’s presence and authority. Orthodox Jewish men wear the kippah at all times; for others it is worn during prayer and religious occasions. The wearing of the kippah is a matter of custom and commitment rather than a Torah command, but it has become a universal symbol of Jewish identity and reverence.

The tallith (or tallit) is a prayer shawl worn by Jewish men during morning prayers. Its corners are fitted with fringes called tzitzit, which are a physical reminder of the 613 commandments. The Torah commands Jews to attach such fringes to their garments so that, when they see them, they will remember all God’s commands. Some Liberal Jewish women also wear the tallith. Like the kippah, the tallith is a ‘wearable theology’ — a religious teaching made tangible in fabric.

Key Fact

The kippah symbolises humility before God — a reminder that God is always above and present. The tallith, with its tzitzit fringes, is a physical reminder of the 613 commandments. Both are examples of Jewish practice embedding theology in everyday life.

The Synagogue: Interior Features

The synagogue is the central building of Jewish communal life — a place of prayer, study and community gathering. Several features of the synagogue interior are of religious significance:

The aron hakodesh (Holy Ark) is a cabinet or alcove set into the wall facing Jerusalem, which holds the Torah scrolls. Opening the ark is a moment of great reverence; the congregation stands when it is opened. The ark is often ornately decorated and may be flanked by carved lions, symbols of the tribe of Judah.

The ner tamid (eternal light) is a lamp that hangs above the ark and burns continuously. It symbolises the eternal nature of God and may also recall the Menorah — the seven-branched lamp that burned in the Temple in Jerusalem. The ner tamid has never been extinguished since it was first lit.

The bimah is the raised platform from which the Torah is read. In Orthodox synagogues it is often placed in the centre of the congregation, so that the words of Torah radiate outward to all present. In Reform synagogues it is commonly at the front, closer to where the ark stands. The Torah scroll is lifted, carried and read from the bimah with great ceremony. Many synagogues also display the words of the Ten Commandments near the ark, signifying the centrality of God’s law to Jewish life.

Shabbat: The Jewish Sabbath

Shabbat (the Sabbath) is the weekly day of rest, observed from Friday evening at sunset to Saturday night when three stars are visible. Exodus 20:8–10 commands: ‘Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work, but the seventh day is a sabbath to the Lord your God.’ Shabbat commemorates two things: God’s rest on the seventh day after creation (Genesis 1–2), and the Israelites’ liberation from slavery in Egypt, where there had been no rest.

Shabbat observance varies considerably between Orthodox and Reform Jews. In Orthodox practice, the prohibitions are extensive: no work, no lighting fires or electricity (which means no cooking, no driving, no using a phone), no writing. The Shabbat is ushered in by the woman of the household lighting two candles, reciting a blessing, and covering her eyes while saying the Hebrew prayer. Kiddush (sanctification) is made over a cup of wine. A double portion of challah bread (recalling the double portion of manna in the wilderness) is shared. Synagogue attendance, family meals and rest define the day.

In Reform and Liberal Judaism, the spirit of Shabbat is honoured while some of the detailed prohibitions are relaxed. A Reform family might drive to synagogue, but still light candles, say Kiddush and observe the day as distinctive and holy. Both approaches see Shabbat as one of Judaism’s greatest gifts — a regular rhythm of rest built into the structure of the week.

Key Fact

Shabbat is commanded in Exodus 20:8–10 and runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. It commemorates both creation and the Exodus. Observance involves candle lighting, Kiddush, challah bread and rest from work — though the extent of prohibitions varies between Orthodox and Reform practice.

Kashrut: The Jewish Dietary Laws

Kashrut (from the root meaning ‘fit’ or ‘proper’) is the system of Jewish food laws. Food that meets these laws is kosher; food that does not is treifa (forbidden). A third category, parev, refers to foods that are neither meat nor dairy and may be eaten with either.

The main rules of kashrut are drawn from Leviticus 11:1–24 and other Torah passages. Land animals must chew the cud and have split hooves (so beef and lamb are kosher; pork is not). Fish must have fins and scales (so shellfish are treifa). Birds of prey are forbidden. Animals must be slaughtered in a specific way called shechitah, performed by a trained shochet (ritual slaughterer) who makes a single swift cut to minimise suffering. The blood must be fully drained before the meat can be eaten, since the Torah forbids the consumption of blood.

One of the most distinctive kashrut rules is the complete separation of milk and meat. This is derived from the Torah’s threefold repetition of the phrase ‘you shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk’ (Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). In practice this means observant Jewish households maintain two separate sets of crockery, cutlery and utensils — one for meat and one for dairy — and a waiting period between eating meat and dairy meals.

Orthodox Jews observe kashrut because it is commanded in the Torah — the word of God — and requires no further justification beyond the command itself. It is also understood to sanctify the act of eating, making a mundane activity into an act of religious obedience. It distinguishes the Jewish community from others and provides a constant, daily practice of self-discipline in obedience to God.

Reform Jews approach kashrut more selectively. Some observe it fully, others partially, and some not at all. The Reform movement generally holds that Jewish ethical principles — such as justice and compassion — are more binding than ritual laws, and that Jews must make their own informed choices about observance. Some Reform Jews apply the ethical spirit of kashrut in modern ways, such as choosing ethically farmed meat, even where traditional rules are relaxed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on Jewish practice, examiners reward explanation of the religious reasons behind a practice, not just a description of what Jews do. For example, if asked about the kippah, don’t just say ‘Jews wear it on their heads’ — explain that it signifies humility before God, the sense of something above the wearer. For kashrut questions, link the food laws to their Torah sources (Leviticus 11:1–24, Exodus 23:19) and explain the significance of shechitah. For Shabbat questions, remember to cite Exodus 20:8–10 and explain the difference between Orthodox and Reform observance as an example of diversity within Judaism.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Shema (‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one’) is Judaism’s central declaration of faith, recited daily. Physical symbols of devotion include the kippah (humility before God) and the tallith with its tzitzit fringes (reminders of the 613 commandments). The synagogue interior features the aron hakodesh (Torah ark), ner tamid (eternal light) and bimah (reading platform).
  • Shabbat (from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall) is commanded in Exodus 20:8–10. It involves candle lighting, Kiddush and rest from work. Orthodox and Reform Jews differ in how strictly they apply the prohibitions.
  • Kashrut (Jewish dietary law) draws on Leviticus 11:1–24. Food must be kosher (permitted), avoiding treifa foods. Shechitah is the required method of slaughter. Milk and meat must be completely separated in an observant kitchen.

practice_questions.text: Describe how observant Jews observe Shabbat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Covers timing (Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall); candle lighting; Kiddush over wine; challah bread; synagogue attendance; rest from work including specific prohibitions; connects to Exodus 20:8-10 and its meaning. Secure: Three or more accurate elements with some explanation. Developing: Two or three elements listed without explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to 'going to synagogue on Saturday' without further detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Shema expresses Jewish beliefs about God.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the Shema's declaration of monotheism ('the Lord is one'); the practice of daily recitation; the role of kavvanah (concentration); explains what it means for Jewish life that God is one (undivided, without rival). Secure: Correct identification of the Shema as an affirmation of monotheism with some explanation of what this means. Developing: Describes the Shema (quotes it) without explaining its theological significance. Emerging: Simple statement that the Shema is a prayer.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which kashrut (Jewish dietary laws) reflects Jewish beliefs about God and the Torah.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed points (e.g. shechitah shows respect for animal life and obedience to God's commands in Leviticus; the milk/meat separation sanctifies everyday eating and connects to the Torah's explicit command in Exodus 23:19). Each point links practice to belief and includes a source. Secure: Two practices correctly identified and linked to belief, with at least one Torah reference. Developing: One practice explained; the second lacks theological connection. Emerging: Description of food rules without any connection to belief.

practice_questions.text: 'Jewish dietary laws are no longer relevant in the modern world.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues for irrelevance (impractical in modern life; health science supersedes ancient prohibitions; Reform Judaism prioritises ethics over ritual; a secular view that food rules belong to a pre-scientific age). Argues against (Torah is eternal and binding; kashrut sanctifies daily life; builds Jewish identity and community; ethical slaughter principles may align with animal welfare concerns). Clear personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides with some sources; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Simple personal view.

lessons.title: Sacred Texts, the Covenant and Jewish Identity
lessons.description: Tenakh and Talmud, the Covenants, brit milah, bar/bat mitzvah and Jewish symbols.
lessons.content_html:
The Tenakh: G-d’s Revealed Word

The Jewish Bible is called the Tenakh, an acronym made from its three sections: Torah (the Five Books of Moses, containing law and narrative), Nevi’im (the Prophets, including books of history and prophetic literature), and Ketuvim (the Writings, including Psalms, Proverbs, and wisdom literature). Together, these texts form the authoritative revealed word of G-d for Jewish people. The Torah in particular holds the highest status — it is handwritten on parchment scrolls, dressed in protective coverings, and stored in the aron hakodesh (the ark) in the synagogue. A metal or ivory pointer called a yad (meaning “hand”) is used when reading, so that human fingers never touch the sacred text.

Jewish communities use the Tenakh in worship (public Torah readings follow a structured annual cycle), in prayer (the Psalms form the backbone of the Jewish prayer book), in study (the Torah is studied intensively in yeshivot and schools), and in celebration (readings mark festivals, weddings, and lifecycle events). Different Jewish movements hold different views on the Tenakh’s origin: Orthodox Jews regard it as the direct, verbatim word of G-d dictated to Moses; Reform and Liberal Jews tend to view it as divinely inspired but shaped by human authors and historical context.

Key Fact

The Torah (Law), Nevi’im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings) together form the Tenakh. The Torah is the most authoritative section, containing the 613 commandments (mitzvot) that observant Jews are called to follow.

The Talmud

The Talmud is the second great body of sacred Jewish literature. It consists of the Mishnah (an early codification of oral law, compiled around the 3rd century CE) and the Gemara (rabbinic commentary and debate on the Mishnah). The Talmud’s purpose is to explain and apply the laws found in the Torah to the full range of human situations — from business ethics to family law to questions of life and death. It is not a simple rulebook; it preserves minority opinions and ongoing debate, on the principle that honest disagreement is itself sacred.

For observant Jews, the Talmud is an indispensable guide to daily life. Major rulings of the Talmud shape practices such as kashrut (dietary laws), Shabbat observance, and lifecycle ceremonies. The Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 contains one of the most famous lines in all of Jewish literature, teaching that one who destroys a single life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and one who saves a single life is as if they saved a whole world. This passage grounds Jewish attitudes to the sanctity of human life. The great medieval scholar Maimonides (known as the Rambam) built on Talmudic tradition to codify Jewish law in his Mishneh Torah and articulate thirteen principles of faith.

The foundational relationship between G-d and the Jewish people is the Covenant. The first great covenant was made with Abraham, recorded in Genesis 12:1–3 and expanded in Genesis 17:6–8. G-d promised Abraham three things: a great nation would descend from him, his descendants would possess the land of Canaan (the Promised Land), and all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. In return, Abraham and his male descendants were to be circumcised as a physical sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:11–14).

The Abrahamic Covenant establishes Jewish identity as both chosen and responsible. Being chosen is not a mark of superiority but of vocation — a calling to live according to G-d’s Torah and to be a blessing to the wider world. The covenant’s promises — land, nationhood, and blessing — remain central to Jewish self-understanding today, even for Jews living in the diaspora far from the land of Israel.

The second great covenant was made through Moses at Sinai. Exodus 3:11–15 records G-d’s call to Moses, where G-d reveals the divine name (YHWH, “I AM WHO I AM”) and commissions Moses to lead the people out of Egypt. At Sinai, G-d gave Israel the Torah, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20), which form the core of Jewish ethical and religious law. The Mosaic Covenant is conditional: Israel receives G-d’s protection and blessing in return for obedience to the Torah.

The Ten Commandments remain central to Jewish life today. They cover duties to G-d (no other gods, no images, Sabbath observance, honouring the divine name) and duties to other people (honouring parents, prohibitions on murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting). Different Jewish communities interpret and apply these commandments differently: Orthodox Jews observe Shabbat very strictly, while Reform communities may take a more flexible approach to how the commandments are fulfilled in modern life.

Jewish Identity: Symbols and Ceremonies

Brit milah (literally “covenant of circumcision”) is one of the oldest and most fundamental Jewish practices. Performed on male infants on the eighth day of life, it is carried out by a trained practitioner called a mohel. The father of the child holds a central role, and a sandek (an honoured guest, often a grandparent) holds the baby during the ceremony. The ritual physically marks every Jewish male as a participant in the covenant made with Abraham, making it an act of both religious significance and family identity.

Jewish boys mark their transition to religious adulthood at the age of 13 through the bar mitzvah ceremony (“son of the commandment”), and girls at 12 or 13 through the bat mitzvah (“daughter of the commandment”). The young person reads from the Torah scroll in the synagogue for the first time, publicly demonstrating their ability to engage with the sacred text and their readiness to take on the full responsibility of the mitzvot. The ceremony is accompanied by celebration with family and community.

Key Fact

Jewish adult males traditionally pray wearing a tallit (prayer shawl) and tefillin (leather boxes containing Torah passages, bound to the arm and forehead). The tallit’s fringes remind the wearer of all the commandments; the tefillin physically bind the words of Torah to the heart and mind.

The Magen David (Shield of David, the six-pointed star) is a widely recognised symbol of Jewish identity, displayed on the Israeli flag and on synagogues worldwide. The mezuzah (doorpost scroll) marks the threshold of a Jewish home. These symbols are not worshipped but serve as constant, visible reminders of the covenant relationship between G-d and the Jewish people.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about Jewish identity ceremonies, examiners want more than a description of what happens — they want you to explain the religious reasons behind the practice. For brit milah, for example, link it to the Abrahamic Covenant in Genesis 17:11–14. For bar/bat mitzvah, explain why the age of 13 is significant (it marks the point at which a Jew becomes personally responsible for the commandments). For the 8-mark ‘Explain Two Beliefs’ question, you might explain two beliefs about the Torah (e.g. Orthodox view: direct word of G-d; Reform view: divinely inspired but shaped by human authors), each with supporting evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Tenakh (Torah, Nevi’im, Ketuvim) is the Jewish Bible and primary source of authority. The Torah holds the highest status as G-d’s law. The Talmud explains and applies Torah law to all aspects of life, preserving rabbinic debate across generations.
  • The Abrahamic Covenant (Genesis 12:1–3, 17:6–8) promised land, nationhood, and blessing; the Mosaic Covenant (Exodus 3:11–15) gave the Torah including the Ten Commandments. Both covenants define Jewish identity as chosen and responsible before G-d.
  • Jewish identity is expressed through ceremonies (brit milah, bar/bat mitzvah) and symbols (tallit, tefillin, mezuzah, Magen David). Each practice connects the individual to the covenant community and to the obligations of Torah.

practice_questions.text: What is the Talmud?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A vast collection of rabbinic debate and legal commentary on the Torah, compiled from the Mishnah (oral law) and Gemara (commentary), used to guide Jewish practice in all areas of life. Developing: A Jewish holy book with laws and rules.

practice_questions.text: Describe the brit milah ceremony and explain its significance for Jewish identity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes the ceremony (eighth day, performed by the mohel, sandek holds the baby, father present) and explains significance (fulfils the Abrahamic Covenant, Genesis 17:11-14; physically marks the child as part of the covenant people; ties the individual to thousands of years of Jewish tradition). Secure: Accurate description with one clear reason for significance. Developing: Partial description, little explanation of significance. Emerging: Vague reference to circumcision as a Jewish practice.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Abrahamic Covenant continues to influence Jewish life and identity today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Genesis 12:1-3 and 17:6-8 cited; links to brit milah as physical sign; influence on Jewish sense of vocation ('chosen' = responsible); role of the covenant in diaspora Jewish identity and connection to Israel. Secure: Identifies the covenant and links it to one or two modern practices or beliefs. Developing: Describes the covenant without connecting to present-day influence. Emerging: Vague mention of Abraham and the Jewish people.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the importance of the Torah, using sources of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) Orthodox: Torah is the direct word of G-d, making every commandment binding; (2) Reform: Torah is divinely inspired but must be interpreted in light of modern ethics — both linked to Talmudic tradition or specific verses. Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source cited and interpreted. Developing: Two beliefs stated but not developed; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'The bar/bat mitzvah ceremony is the most important moment in a Jewish person's life.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: marks full entry into religious adulthood, first public Torah reading, lifelong responsibility for mitzvot begins — deeply significant religiously. Disagree: brit milah (physical covenant sign from birth) and marriage might be equally important; some liberal Jews question gender distinctions; for non-practising Jews the ceremony may be cultural rather than spiritual. Non-religious view: secular transitions (e.g. turning 18) are more legally meaningful; the ceremony carries cultural rather than spiritual weight. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with at least two sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or superficial. Emerging: Simple assertion.

lessons.title: Jewish Festivals: Pesach, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
lessons.description: How and why Jews observe Yom Hashoah, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach.
lessons.content_html:
The Jewish Festival Calendar

The Jewish year is marked by a rich cycle of festivals and commemorations, each rooted in the Torah and in historical experience. Festivals serve multiple purposes: they renew the relationship with G-d, transmit Jewish identity across generations, commemorate historical events, and provide structured moments for repentance, joy, and remembrance. This lesson covers four of the most significant: Yom Hashoah, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Pesach (Passover).

Yom Hashoah: Holocaust Remembrance

Yom Hashoah (“Day of the Holocaust”) is observed on the 27th of Nisan in the Hebrew calendar, in spring. It was established by the Israeli parliament (Knesset) in 1953 to honour the memory of the approximately six million Jewish men, women, and children murdered by the Nazi regime between 1933 and 1945. In Israel, air-raid sirens sound across the country, and the entire nation falls silent for two minutes. Memorial ceremonies take place in synagogues, schools, and community centres across Britain and around the world.

The commemoration involves the lighting of six yellow candles, representing the six million victims. Survivors and their families share testimony; the phrase “Never Again” (Lo Yishaney) captures the determination that the lessons of the Holocaust must be kept alive. Yom Hashoah has particular theological significance: it raises profound questions about theodicy (how a just G-d could permit such suffering), and some Jewish thinkers have responded by emphasising human responsibility and the obligation to pursue justice. The day also reinforces the importance of the State of Israel as a homeland and refuge for the Jewish people.

Key Fact

Yom Hashoah (Holocaust Remembrance Day) is observed on the 27th of Nisan. Six yellow candles are lit to represent the six million Jewish victims of the Holocaust. The day raises questions of theodicy and reinforces the phrase “Never Again.”

Rosh Hashanah: The Jewish New Year

Rosh Hashanah (“Head of the Year”) falls on the first and second days of Tishrei (September or October). It marks the Jewish New Year and, according to tradition, the anniversary of the creation of the world. Rosh Hashanah is also understood as the beginning of the period of divine judgement: tradition teaches that on this day G-d opens three books — one for the wholly righteous, one for the wholly wicked, and one for those in between. Most people fall into the third category, and they have ten days (the “Days of Awe”) to repent before the books are sealed on Yom Kippur.

The central symbol of Rosh Hashanah is the shofar — a ram’s horn blown in the synagogue during prayer. The shofar’s sound is a call to wake up and examine one’s life before G-d. It is blown in a sequence of notes that include a long wailing sound (tekiah gedolah), symbolising the urgent need for repentance. The synagogue service on Rosh Hashanah is longer than usual, including special liturgical poems (piyyutim) and prayers.

Traditional foods for Rosh Hashanah include apples dipped in honey, symbolising the hope for a sweet new year. Round challah bread (rather than the usual plaited form) symbolises the cycle of the year. The greeting “Shanah tovah” (“a good year”) is exchanged among Jewish people throughout this period.

Yom Kippur: The Day of Atonement

Yom Kippur (“Day of Atonement”) falls ten days after Rosh Hashanah and is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. It is a day of solemn fasting — observant Jews abstain from food and drink, washing for pleasure, wearing leather shoes, using cosmetics, and marital relations for approximately 25 hours, from before sunset until after dark the following evening. The fast is a physical sign of humility and self-examination before G-d.

Synagogue services on Yom Kippur last for much of the day. The evening service, known as Kol Nidre (named after the haunting prayer that opens it), is one of the most attended services of the Jewish year. Many Jews who do not attend synagogue at any other time come for Kol Nidre. The day culminates in Ne’ilah, the “closing” service, representing the closing of the heavenly gates. The shofar is blown one final time to mark the end of Yom Kippur. Jews emerge from the fast with the hope that their repentance has been accepted and their names inscribed in the Book of Life.

Key Fact

Yom Kippur is the holiest day of the Jewish year. Observant Jews fast for approximately 25 hours and spend much of the day in synagogue, culminating in the Ne’ilah service. The shofar is blown at the end of the fast. It completes the ten Days of Awe that begin at Rosh Hashanah.

Pesach (Passover) is the spring festival commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, described in the book of Exodus and commanded to be observed “for ever” in Exodus 12:14. It lasts for seven days (eight in the diaspora). Preparation begins weeks in advance: the home must be thoroughly cleaned to remove all chametz (leavened products). This cleansing is symbolic as well as practical — it represents removing spiritual as well as physical “puffing up.”

The central ritual of Pesach is the Seder meal, held on the first (and in the diaspora, second) night of Pesach. The word seder means “order” — the meal follows a strict sequence. Participants read from the Haggadah (“telling”), which retells the Exodus story through narrative, songs, questions, and discussion. The youngest child present asks the Four Questions, beginning with “Why is this night different from all other nights?”

The Seder plate holds symbolic foods: bitter herbs (maror) representing the bitterness of slavery; a lamb shank bone representing the Passover sacrifice; a roasted egg representing sacrifice and mourning; charoset (a paste of fruit and nuts) representing mortar used by slaves; parsley or another vegetable representing spring and hope; and a second bitter vegetable. Matzah (unleavened bread) replaces chametz throughout the festival, remembering that the Israelites left Egypt in such haste that their bread had no time to rise.

There is considerable diversity in how Jews observe these festivals. Orthodox communities observe Pesach for eight days and maintain strict standards for identifying chametz; Reform communities may observe seven days and apply less restrictive food standards. For Yom Kippur, some non-observant Jews attend Kol Nidre as a cultural practice even if they do not fast. Rosh Hashanah observance ranges from full-day synagogue attendance in Orthodox communities to a family meal and card-sending in more secular households. This diversity reflects the broad spectrum of Jewish identity in Britain today, from strictly Orthodox communities to fully secular cultural Jews.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about Jewish festivals, always explain the theological significance of the practice, not just what people do. For Pesach, link Exodus 12:14 (“a lasting ordinance”) to the idea that every generation is meant to see themselves as having personally been freed from Egypt — this is stated in the Haggadah. For the 15-mark question on whether festivals are the most important part of Jewish life, you could argue both ways: festivals connect Jews to their history and to G-d (agree), but Torah study and Shabbat observance form the weekly backbone of Jewish life (disagree). Remember to include a non-religious perspective.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Yom Hashoah (Holocaust Remembrance) is observed on the 27th of Nisan with six candles and two minutes of silence. Rosh Hashanah (New Year) begins the Days of Awe with the shofar; Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) ends them with fasting and the Ne’ilah service.
  • Pesach (Passover) commemorates the Exodus commanded in Exodus 12:14. Preparation involves removing all chametz; the Seder meal uses the Haggadah to retell the Exodus story, and matzah replaces leavened bread throughout the festival.
  • Festival observance varies significantly between Orthodox, Reform, and secular Jewish communities, reflecting the diversity of Jewish identity in Britain today.

practice_questions.text: Give two foods placed on the Pesach Seder plate and state what each one represents.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each correct food with its meaning: bitter herbs (maror) = bitterness of slavery; lamb shank bone = Passover sacrifice; roasted egg = sacrifice/mourning; charoset = mortar used by slaves; parsley = spring and hope. Any two correct pairs for full marks.

practice_questions.text: What is the shofar?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A ram's horn blown as a musical instrument during Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, whose sound calls Jews to repentance and self-examination before G-d. Developing: A horn blown at Jewish festivals.

practice_questions.text: Describe how Jews observe Yom Kippur and explain why it is considered the holiest day of the year.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes fasting (~25 hours), abstaining from other pleasures, Kol Nidre evening service, Ne'ilah closing service, final shofar blast; explains holiness as the day the heavenly books are sealed, completing repentance begun at Rosh Hashanah, the climax of the ten Days of Awe. Secure: Accurate description of two or more elements with one reason for significance. Developing: Partial description; reason for holiness absent or vague. Emerging: Vague reference to Yom Kippur as a fast day.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Pesach reinforces Jewish identity and connects Jews to their history.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Links Exodus 12:14 to the command to observe Pesach 'for ever'; explains how the Seder retells the Exodus story so every generation identifies with the freed slaves; removal of chametz as physical and spiritual renewal; matzah as reminder of haste and dependence on G-d. Secure: Two clear ways Pesach connects Jews to history with some explanation. Developing: One way described without full explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to Passover celebrating freedom.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about repentance, using sources of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) Repentance (teshuvah) must be sincere and followed by changed behaviour — the ten Days of Awe give time for this before Yom Kippur seals the divine judgement; (2) G-d is merciful and forgives genuine repentance — supported by the tradition of three divine books at Rosh Hashanah. Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source. Developing: Two beliefs stated briefly; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'Yom Kippur is more important for Jewish identity than Pesach.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: Yom Kippur is the holiest day; it culminates the Days of Awe; Kol Nidre draws even secular Jews; atonement is central to the Jewish relationship with G-d. Disagree: Pesach is commanded in Exodus 12:14 as an eternal ordinance; it connects Jews to the foundational Exodus narrative; the Seder transmits faith within families across generations; it is widely practised even in non-observant households. Non-religious view: neither has spiritual significance; both are cultural traditions expressing community identity. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with at least two sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or weak sources. Emerging: Simple assertion.

The Jewish New Year, observed on the first day of Tishrei, marking the anniversary of creation and the beginning of the ten Days of Awe.
A ram's horn blown as a musical instrument during Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, whose sound calls Jews to repentance.
The Day of Atonement, observed on the 10th of Tishrei — the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, devoted to fasting and prayer.
The act of going without food or drink for a set period as an act of self-discipline, humility, and devotion to G-d.
The spring festival commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, commanded in Exodus 12:14.
Leavened bread or any food containing a leavening agent, forbidden in Jewish homes during Pesach.
The ceremonial meal held on the first night(s) of Pesach, during which the story of the Exodus is retold using the Haggadah.
The book that guides the Pesach Seder, retelling the story of the Exodus through prayers, songs, and symbolic foods.
The ceremonial plate used at the Pesach Seder, holding symbolic foods that represent the Exodus story.
Unleavened flatbread eaten during Pesach, representing the haste with which the Israelites left Egypt.
